tagline: Mexico to Canada in an afternoon, by way of Mount Graham.
intro: SR 366 leaves US 191 south of Safford in cactus and mesquite at 2,900 feet and runs straight for the Pinaleño Mountains, the highest of southeastern Arizona's sky islands. Then it starts to climb, through oak grassland and pinyon and juniper, into pine, and at last spruce and fir on the 9,000-foot ridges. The Forest Service calls it the ecological equivalent of driving from Mexico to Canada.

The road is named for T. T. Swift, first supervisor of the Coronado National Forest. The Civilian Conservation Corps built it during the Depression, along with many of the campgrounds and trails it reaches.

moments.title: Turkey Flat
moments.text: One of two cabin communities the road serves, and the place where it takes five hairpin turns in a row.

moments.title: Columbine
moments.text: The other cabin community, near where the state highway runs out, with a visitor center on the edge of an alpine meadow.

moments.title: Riggs Flat Lake
moments.text: At the end of the road, an 11-acre lake in alpine forest and meadow, its cold water stocked with trout in summer.

practical: The pavement ends partway up and the upper road continues on gravel. The Forest Service closes the Swift Trail for the winter, from November 15 to April 15, and does not recommend vehicles longer than 22 feet on its switchbacks.
